query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, adherent spray-deposited coating of 2D HEA nanoflakes (similar in composition to (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2) onto a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy substrate will induce in situ formation of an adaptive, lubricious tribolayer under sliding that maintains low friction coefficients and wear rates from room temperature up to 800 °C under varying loads and environmental conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix in its as-processed, untreated state, exhibiting baseline tribological behavior with relatively high friction and wear challenges at both low and high temperatures.
generation.intervention: A single intervention of applying a spray deposition of a thin, adherent 2D HEA nanoflake coating onto the CoCrFeNi surface.
generation.conditions: Sliding (ball-on-disk) tribological tests conducted in ambient air over a temperature range of room temperature to 800 °C and under variable loads (including high contact pressures around 0.9–1 GPa).
generation.structural_mediator: An engineered, layered nanoflake coating that, upon sliding, reorganizes to form a continuous, adaptive tribolayer.
generation.mechanism: Under mechanical shear, the 2D HEA nanoflake coating undergoes tribocatalytic reorganization to form a lubricious oxide/tribolayer. This dynamic layer adjusts its structure to accommodate changes in temperature and load, thereby reducing direct metal-metal contact, mitigating oxidation, and evenly distributing stress.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated CoCrFeNi system will exhibit significantly lower coefficients of friction and reduced wear rates across the full temperature range compared to the uncoated baseline. A failure would be indicated if the friction and wear performance remain similar to the untreated material at any test condition.
generation.baseline: The untreated CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, which shows increased friction and wear challenges at high temperatures and under variable loads.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective in ambient air across temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C and under moderate to high contact pressures (~0.9–1 GPa). Its performance under prolonged cyclical loading and extremely aggressive environments remains to be determined.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the long-term stability of the spray-deposited nanoflake coating, its resistance to degradation under extreme cyclic stress, and potential variations in lubrication effectiveness based on subtle changes in environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of CoCrFeNi substrates coated with the 2D HEA nanoflake spray and one set left uncoated as the baseline. Conduct ball-on-disk sliding tests across temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C under a range of controlled loads (targeting ~0.9–1 GPa contact pressure) in ambient air.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) as a function of temperature and load
Wear rate (mm³/N·m) measured from wear track analysis
Surface and cross-sectional microscopy to analyze tribolayer formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both COF and wear rate over the full temperature range compared to the uncoated baseline, or if the expected adaptive tribolayer is absent or unstable under any of the tested conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. AbstractHigh Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have garnered attention due to their remarkable tribological attributes. Predominantly, failure mechanisms in HEAs emanate from stress‐induced dislocations, culminating in crack propagation and film delamination. In this study, we report on the synthesis of 2D HEA of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 which facilitates shear‐induced energy dissipation at sliding interfaces. The ball‐on‐disk tribological investigations demonstrate unprecedentedly low average coefficients of friction (0.076) and wear rates (10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1) under high contact pressures (0.936 GPa) within ambient conditions. Employing multi‐scale characterizations alongside molecular dynamic simulations, we elucidate that the presence of the HEA triggers tribocatalytic activity under high contact pressures emerging as a pivotal factor in extending lubricant lifespan during tribological tests. The resilient lubriciousness coupled with the facile spray coating methodology of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 in ambient environments paves the way for the development of a new class of solid lubricants based on 2D HEA. In this study, we successfully synthesized a transition metal dichalcogenide high entropy alloy of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 with 2D structure and tested its tribological properties by performing ball‐on‐disk friction experiments using steel against steel tribopair in an ambient environment. The lubricant was coated onto the steel substrate by the conventional air spray coating process. The lubricant displayed excellent tribological properties with low average coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rates of ≈0.076 and 2.6 × 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1, respectively, at the high load of 9 N (contact pressure: 0.936 GPa). The analyses performed on the wear track and wear debris indicate stress‐induced tribocatalytic activity that facilitates the self‐lubricating behavior of HEA nanoflakes during friction tests performed in ambient conditions.

Intrigued by the extensive lubricious behavior of the HEA in ethanol, a further study has been conducted to analyze the capabilities of HEA nanoflakes in other solvents like water. The (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 powder is combined with distilled water at a concentration of 1.5g L−1. This water‐based lubricant solution was sonicated for thorough mixing (≈9 h sonication time) and spray coated uniformly onto the steel disk for ball‐on‐disk friction experiments across all loads from 1 N to 9 N. The results found all sliding tests to fail within short distances (Figure S5, Supporting Information). In Figure S5 (Supporting Information), the starting COF decreases with an increase in load, showing the intrinsic HEA behavior like in the case of HEA in ethanol. However, the HEA in water exhibits limited wear resistance and high wear rates in the magnitude of 10−6 mm3 (N∙m)−1 as compared to HEA in ethanol which has wear rates in the magnitude of 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1. This shows that the ethanol solvent plays a significant role in increasing the tribological performance of HEA during friction tests. In summary, we developed a novel solid lubricant based on the 2D HEA structure, which combines the advantages of HEAs enhanced mechanical properties and low‐shearing behavior of 2D materials to demonstrate a superior self‐lubricating behavior. The comprehensive post‐test characterizations coupled with MD simulation studies revealed interesting tribochemistry at play leading to the dissociation of entrapped ethanol molecules and converting it into a‐C in the presence of catalytically active HEA nanoflakes, which are responsible for the formation of tribolayer, wherein the full lubricious behavior was complemented by the retained HEA nanoflakes. This discovery opens up a new avenue to develop advanced solid lubricants based on 2D HEA with high compositional flexibility and low‐shear‐strength layered structure for oil‐free tribological systems. The other important aspect of the 2D HEA lubricant developed in this study is the ability to coat the given surface using a simple spray coating technique. proposals.intervention: Apply a thin, adherent coating of 2D HEA nanoflakes akin to (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 via spray deposition
proposals.conditions: Sliding tests conducted under varying loads (e.g., ~0.9 GPa contact pressure) and temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C in ambient air
proposals.structural_mediator: A tribo-catalytically active, layered nanoflake coating
proposals.mechanism: Under sliding contact, the 2D nanoflake coating activates shear-induced reorganization to form a lubricious tribofilm that adapts to temperature variations. At lower temperatures, its inherent low friction is expressed, while at higher temperatures, the coating’s stable layered structure promotes formation of a continuous lubricious oxide/tribolayer, mitigating adhesive and oxidative wear.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the plain CoCrFeNi substrate, the coated system will show significantly lower coefficients of friction and wear rates uniformly over the entire temperature range. A failure of the hypothesis would be indicated by comparable friction/wear performance to the uncoated material at any temperature.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention directly targets lubrication across a broad temperature range by introducing a dynamic, adaptive coating that compensates for the inherent limitations of the bare CoCrFeNi matrix under varied conditions.

proposals.material_system: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with engineered precipitates
proposals.intervention: Introduce controlled nano-oxide precipitates via a post-sintering aging treatment
proposals.conditions: A controlled heat treatment in air or inert atmosphere (e.g., 650–750 °C for varying times) is applied after alloy consolidation and prior to tribological testing under loads representative of practical use (e.g., moderate to high contact pressures) and temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C
proposals.structural_mediator: Nano-oxide precipitates homogeneously dispersed in the alloy matrix and near-surface region
proposals.mechanism: The nano-oxides act as stable, hard second phases that pin the grain boundaries and promote the formation of an adaptive, nanocrystalline glaze layer during sliding. This glaze layer can accommodate thermal expansion and protect against adhesive and oxidative wear across the tested temperature range.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The precipitate-engineered CoCrFeNi will exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates over the full temperature span compared to the baseline alloy. If no significant improvement in friction and wear is observed, the hypothesis will be falsified.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By modifying the internal microstructure with nano-oxides, the system can dynamically generate protective tribofilms during sliding, thereby ensuring low friction and wear across diverse temperature, load, and environmental conditions.

proposals.material_system: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy pre-processed by severe plastic deformation
proposals.intervention: Apply severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion) followed by a low-temperature annealing step to produce an ultra-fine grained surface layer
proposals.conditions: The alloy is deformed at room temperature using high-pressure torsion under defined pressure and rotation speed, then annealed at a temperature low enough (e.g., 600 °C) to stabilize the refined microstructure without significant grain growth. Tribological tests are performed from room temperature to 800 °C under representative loads in inert or ambient environments
proposals.structural_mediator: An ultrafine or nanocrystalline surface and near-surface layer with high grain boundary density
proposals.mechanism: The refined grain structure leads to an inverse Hall-Petch effect where the high density of grain boundaries facilitates dynamic amorphization and formation of a resilient, adaptive tribolayer during sliding. This layer is capable of accommodating high-temperature oxidation and stress, thus reducing friction and wear over a wide temperature range.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The ultra-fine grained CoCrFeNi will show uniformly lower friction and wear compared to coarse-grained counterparts. Failure of the hypothesis would be indicated if the tribological behavior deteriorates at high temperatures (e.g., due to grain growth or inadequate stabilization).
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach leverages microstructural grain refinement to inherently improve surface mechanics, ensuring robust tribological performance across a broad range of operating conditions.

proposals.intervention: Implement laser surface texturing to create micro- and nano-scale patterns on the alloy surface
proposals.conditions: Laser texturing is performed under controlled atmospheres (e.g., inert gas or ambient air) with optimized pulsed laser parameters (e.g., fluence, pulse duration, and repetition rate) to produce regular microgrooves and nanopits. Subsequent ball-on-disk tests are carried out across room temperature to 800 °C under varying loads
proposals.structural_mediator: A laser-induced textured surface featuring patterned micro/nanostructures
proposals.mechanism: The surface texturing creates reservoirs for wear debris and facilitates in situ formation of lubricious oxide films at high temperatures. The patterned architecture also promotes controlled stress distribution and limits direct contact area, thereby lowering friction and wear.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Textured surfaces will maintain comparatively lower friction coefficients and wear rates throughout the temperature range, relative to untreated surfaces. Conversely, if the texturing leads to increased stress concentrations or fails to stabilize lubricant layer formation at high temperature, the hypothesis is refuted.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: Surface texturing offers a physical, controllable means to manage contact mechanics and tribofilm formation, directly addressing the challenge of achieving stable tribological properties under both low and high temperatures.

decision.rationale: Direction B was chosen because it directly addresses the challenge of maintaining low friction and wear over a wide temperature range by applying a thin, adaptive 2D HEA nanoflake coating. The mechanism of tribocatalytically activating a lubricious, layered tribofilm is strongly supported by prior evidence (e.g., PMC12019924) demonstrating extremely low friction coefficients and wear rates under high loads. Although each candidate has merit, the 2D nanoflake coating approach leverages recent successes in self‐lubricating 2D HEA systems and provides a clear pathway for adaptation under varied environmental conditions without presupposing an intervention class.
